booking-totals.subject: Booking ledger A
facts: The summary lists $60,000 of room charges for a twelve-month period.
The supplied transaction lines total $54,000, with a separate $6,000 cleaning-charge subtotal.
The glossary does not say whether the headline includes cleaning receipts.
booking-totals.principle: A room-charge claim needs a consistent transaction classification. The two displayed totals can be reconciled only after the receipt types are separated.
booking-totals.risk: A mixed headline can distort every rate or return calculation using it.
booking-totals.deliverable: a transaction bridge identifying which receipt categories belong in the claimed room-charge measure

payout-reconciliation.subject: Payout bridge A
facts: The reservation ledger lists $50,000 in room charges.
The payout statement totals $43,000 after deductions and timing adjustments.
The comparison note calls the $7,000 difference missing revenue without reviewing the adjustment lines.
payout-reconciliation.principle: A gross charge total and a net payout are different measures. A difference is a question for reconciliation, not proof that money is missing.
payout-reconciliation.risk: An unexplained gross-to-net gap can become an unsupported accusation or an incorrect performance summary.
payout-reconciliation.deliverable: a labeled bridge for fees, refunds, collected amounts and timing adjustments

cleaning-pass-through.subject: Cleaning schedule A
facts: Guest cleaning charges total $10,500 across 70 stays.
The cleaner cost illustration is $170 per stay, or $11,900 across those stays.
The operating summary adds cleaning receipts to income but omits the cleaner cost.
cleaning-pass-through.principle: The receipt and its related cost need to be visible together. In this illustration, the listed cleaning amounts imply a $1,400 shortfall before other turnover costs.
cleaning-pass-through.risk: Treating the receipt as pure profit overstates the contribution shown by the example.
cleaning-pass-through.deliverable: a consistent cleaning receipt, turnover count and cost reconciliation

refund-adjustments.subject: Refund ledger A
facts: The booking export includes $52,000 of charges before refunds.
The refund schedule contains $4,000 of reversed charges.
The headline keeps $52,000 while the supporting note describes a post-refund measure.
refund-adjustments.principle: A pre-refund charge total should not be labeled as the post-refund result. The status and reporting cutoff need to match.
refund-adjustments.risk: Different cancellation and refund treatments can make source and summary figures appear to disagree.
refund-adjustments.deliverable: a booking-status reconciliation with refunds and the intended reporting cutoff explicitly shown

occupancy-denominator.subject: Occupancy comparison A
facts: The calendar shows 200 booked nights, 20 owner-use nights and 15 closure nights within 365 calendar nights.
One report uses 365 as the denominator; another uses 330 offered nights.
The comparison calls the two occupancy figures contradictory without stating their definitions.
occupancy-denominator.principle: The same booked-night count can produce two valid measures under different availability definitions. The denominator must travel with the percentage.
occupancy-denominator.risk: An unexplained occupancy comparison can imply a demand difference that is actually a definition difference.
occupancy-denominator.deliverable: a calendar-night bridge and a label for the specific occupancy denominator

nightly-rate-average.subject: Rate average A
facts: Period A has 20 booked nights at $300, producing $6,000 of room charges.
Period B has 80 booked nights at $200, producing $16,000 of room charges.
The summary averages the two rates to $250 instead of dividing $22,000 by 100 booked nights.
nightly-rate-average.principle: The weighted room rate in this illustration is $220. Averaging period rates equally gives a different measure because the night counts differ.
nightly-rate-average.risk: A simple average can overstate or understate the rate generated by the actual mix of booked nights.
nightly-rate-average.deliverable: the room-charge and booked-night weights used to calculate the stated average

revpar-definition.subject: Available-night metric A
facts: The room-charge schedule totals $50,000 with 200 booked nights.
The availability record lists 330 offered nights.
The dashboard labels $250 as revenue per available night even though it divides by booked nights.
revpar-definition.principle: Dividing by booked nights gives a room rate, while dividing by offered nights gives a different metric. The formula, label and period need to align.
revpar-definition.risk: A mislabeled rate can make an operating metric appear stronger than its stated definition supports.
revpar-definition.deliverable: a formula trace showing which nights divide the matching room-revenue amount

partial-year-annualization.subject: Annualization example A
facts: Three observed months produce $24,000 of room charges.
A presentation multiplies the $8,000 monthly average by twelve to show $96,000.
No observations for the other nine months are supplied in this example.
partial-year-annualization.principle: The $96,000 figure is an extrapolation under a constant-month assumption, not an observed annual result.
partial-year-annualization.risk: A mathematically correct multiplication can still be described too strongly when the unobserved period is hidden.
partial-year-annualization.deliverable: a clear separation of the recorded period, the extrapolation formula and unobserved months

seasonal-mix.subject: Seasonal evidence A
facts: The strongest quarter contains $24,000 in room charges.
The remaining nine months contain $18,000 in total room charges.
The presentation discusses only the strongest quarter when describing the year's operation.
seasonal-mix.principle: The selected quarter is part of a $42,000 annual illustration, not a substitute for the full-cycle view. Period selection matters to the conclusion.
seasonal-mix.risk: A narrow sample can conceal weaker months and their funding implications.
seasonal-mix.deliverable: a complete monthly schedule and an explanation of why any selected interval is being discussed

comparable-selection-bias.subject: Comparable register A
facts: The candidate register contains twelve properties that initially meet the search filters.
The published set includes only the four highest room-revenue examples.
The exclusions column is blank for the eight omitted records.
comparable-selection-bias.principle: A selected set is not automatically representative of the candidate set. A documented rule is needed to interpret what the chosen examples show.
comparable-selection-bias.risk: The comparison can be driven by outcome-based selection rather than property similarity.
comparable-selection-bias.deliverable: the candidate list, inclusion rule and property-specific exclusion explanations

management-fee-base.subject: Management invoice A
facts: The example agreement illustration applies 20% to $50,000 of defined room revenue.
The model instead applies 20% to $60,000 including another receipt category.
The summary quotes only the 20% rate and does not show the base.
management-fee-base.principle: The percentage is unchanged but the modeled dollar charge differs by $2,000 because its base differs. The base is part of the fee definition.
management-fee-base.risk: A fee comparison can look aligned while using materially different billing amounts.
management-fee-base.deliverable: a fee-base definition tied to the current scope and a reproducible sample calculation

platform-charges.subject: Channel cost A
facts: Channel A contributes $35,000 of room revenue under a hypothetical 3% fee assumption.
Channel B contributes $15,000 under a hypothetical 10% fee assumption.
The summary applies 3% to the combined $50,000 without explaining the mixed channel assumptions.
platform-charges.principle: The supplied assumptions imply $2,550, not $1,500, in combined modeled charges. These are example rates rather than current platform terms.
platform-charges.risk: A blended channel portfolio can be understated by applying the smallest assumed rate to every receipt.
platform-charges.deliverable: a channel-by-channel fee bridge using the actual applicable definitions and clearly labeled assumptions

utility-schedule.subject: Utility cost A
facts: The supplied bills show $300 in one low-use month and $700 in another month.
The model multiplies only the $300 bill by twelve.
Ten months are unprovided, and the occupancy pattern of the prior owner is unspecified.
utility-schedule.principle: A single observed month supports that month's bill. Multiplying it into an annual amount introduces an assumption about unobserved use and periods.
utility-schedule.risk: A precise annual total can look recorded even when most months were never examined.
utility-schedule.deliverable: a month-by-month bill schedule with missing periods and estimates explicitly labeled

insurance-estimate.subject: Insurance cost evidence A
facts: The expense model uses a historic $2,400 premium from an earlier ownership period.
A current inquiry about the proposed rental use remains open.
The summary describes the historic amount as the buyer's confirmed annual cost.
insurance-estimate.principle: An old premium is a source observation, not confirmation of a current policy for a different use or owner.
insurance-estimate.risk: A cost estimate can be mistaken for coverage confirmation when its scope and date are omitted.
insurance-estimate.deliverable: a current insurer response and an expense assumption labeled to match what has actually been quoted

property-tax-estimate.subject: Property-tax assumption A
facts: The operating model uses a seller's historic $5,000 payment.
The evidence packet does not explain the period, basis or whether the proposed purchase changes the relevant assumptions.
The summary describes the amount as a settled future buyer expense.
property-tax-estimate.principle: A historic payment and a prospective tax assumption are different statements. The example requires appropriate property-specific review rather than a universal rule.
property-tax-estimate.risk: An expense can appear certain when its current basis has not been examined.
property-tax-estimate.deliverable: the relevant authority record and qualified review of the assumption used for the proposed transaction

repair-allowance.subject: Repair comparison A
facts: The model includes a $3,000 repair allowance.
A scoped contractor illustration totals $5,500 and excludes additional investigation.
The summary treats the allowance as if it were the contractor's complete fixed price.
repair-allowance.principle: An internal allowance and a provider's scoped estimate are different records. The amount and exclusions need a bridge before the two are treated as equivalent.
repair-allowance.risk: An allowance can hide both a known difference and still-unpriced work.
repair-allowance.deliverable: a scope-and-amount reconciliation preserving the contractor's exclusions and the owner's separate allowance

reserve-treatment.subject: Reserve movement A
facts: The owner earmarks $10,000 as reserve cash.
Later, $3,000 is paid for work from that cash pool.
The summary subtracts both the full allocation and the $3,000 payment as if they were independent operating expenses.
reserve-treatment.principle: A cash earmark and a subsequent transaction are separate events. The model should show how it treats each without silently counting the same amount twice.
reserve-treatment.risk: Reserve presentation can distort a cash-flow comparison if allocations and uses are mixed.
reserve-treatment.deliverable: a movement schedule distinguishing earmarking, transfers and actual paid or recognized work

capital-work.subject: Capital-work schedule A
capital-work.field: irregular work omitted from cash view
facts: The recurring expense summary totals $25,000.
A separate work schedule identifies a $12,000 irregular project expected during the example period.
The headline cash-flow claim does not mention that separate cash requirement.
capital-work.principle: A recurring-cost measure can be useful, but it does not automatically include irregular work. A cash conclusion should state which obligations remain outside it.
capital-work.risk: An operating result can be mistaken for all cash available to the owner.
capital-work.deliverable: a separate timing and funding schedule for irregular work, with appropriate professional treatment of accounting questions

total-cash-invested.subject: Entry-cost evidence A
facts: The acquisition example has $100,000 down payment, $12,000 closing cash, $30,000 setup, $5,000 fees and $15,000 reserves.
The return summary uses only the $100,000 down payment as its denominator.
The text calls that denominator total cash invested.
total-cash-invested.principle: The listed cash commitments add to $162,000 under the stated definition. A down-payment-only measure needs a different label from an all-cash measure.
total-cash-invested.risk: The same cash-flow numerator can produce a materially different percentage when the denominator changes.
total-cash-invested.deliverable: a component schedule that reconciles the return denominator and identifies any financed, credited or excluded items

deposit-credits.subject: Deposit reconciliation A
facts: The closing illustration requires $112,000 before the deposit credit.
The deposit record shows $10,000 paid earlier.
The summary includes the deposit as a separate cost and also requests the full uncredited $112,000.
deposit-credits.principle: The deposit needs one trace through the cash bridge. Its treatment cannot be inferred solely from its appearance on two separate records.
deposit-credits.risk: An already-paid amount can be counted again or missed entirely when the cash bridge is absent.
deposit-credits.deliverable: the settlement professional's reconciliation of paid deposit, credit applied and additional funds due

purchase-credits.subject: Purchase credit A
facts: The fictional contract price is $400,000 and a credit illustration is $5,000.
The cash bridge applies the credit once to the relevant closing requirement.
A performance summary subtracts it again from a price measure without explaining the different basis.
purchase-credits.principle: Price, credits and funds due are different fields. Each use of a credit needs an explicit definition so it is not silently applied twice.
purchase-credits.risk: An unexplained credit can make cash and yield comparisons inconsistent.
purchase-credits.deliverable: a transaction-specific bridge showing where the credit applies and which measures remain unchanged
recordLabels: Second credit adjustment in performance summary

fee-timing.subject: Service fee schedule A
facts: An example service fee of $5,000 is paid before closing.
The entry-cost summary includes only amounts paid on closing day.
The text describes that summary as all cash committed to acquisition and launch.
fee-timing.principle: Payment date alone does not determine whether an amount belongs in a defined committed-cash measure. The measure needs a stated time and scope boundary.
fee-timing.risk: Upfront amounts can disappear from a denominator simply because they were paid earlier.
fee-timing.deliverable: a fee schedule with recipient, milestone, payment date and inclusion in the chosen cash definition

loan-payment.subject: Loan structure A
facts: The model uses $300,000 principal, a 7% annual rate and thirty-year amortization.
A comparison term illustration describes an initial interest-only period at the same principal and rate.
The summary treats their first monthly payments as the same loan structure.
loan-payment.principle: A principal-and-interest payment and an interest-only payment reflect different repayment structures even when principal and rate match.
loan-payment.risk: A lower initial payment may be extrapolated beyond the period it actually describes.
loan-payment.deliverable: a lender-confirmed payment schedule that identifies principal, interest, repayment structure and later changes

interest-only-period.subject: Payment-period evidence A
facts: The loan illustration has twelve initial interest-only months.
The later period is described as amortizing under separate terms.
The operating summary uses the initial payment amount for every year in its holding scenario.
interest-only-period.principle: One period's payment does not establish every later period's obligation. The change point and later assumptions need to remain visible.
interest-only-period.risk: An initial payment can make long-run financing costs appear more certain or lower than the stated structure supports.
interest-only-period.deliverable: a period-by-period lender schedule and an explicit label for any later payment still being assumed

balloon-balance.subject: Maturity example A
facts: The term illustration uses a thirty-year amortization basis but an earlier maturity date.
A level-payment schedule therefore does not by itself show the full obligation at maturity.
The narrative assumes refinancing will remove the remaining balance without evidence of future financing availability.
balloon-balance.principle: Amortization and maturity describe different features. A future refinance is an assumption rather than an established source of funds.
balloon-balance.risk: A cash-flow narrative can omit a material remaining principal obligation.
balloon-balance.deliverable: the actual maturity terms, remaining-balance illustration and a separately labeled refinancing assumption

debt-service-ratio.subject: Coverage ratio A
facts: The operating-income illustration is $30,000 per year.
The loan-payment line is $2,000 per month.
The summary divides $30,000 by $2,000 and reports a ratio of fifteen without aligning periods.
debt-service-ratio.principle: Annualizing the stated monthly debt gives $24,000 and a ratio of 1.25 under these definitions. Unit alignment is necessary before the ratio is interpreted.
debt-service-ratio.risk: A period mismatch can radically change a headline coverage figure.
debt-service-ratio.deliverable: a formula trace with matching income and debt periods and the lender's relevant income definition

return-denominator.subject: Return basis A
facts: The same $10,000 annual cash-flow illustration is compared with $100,000 down payment and $162,000 total listed cash.
One presentation displays 10% and another about 6.17%.
The summary calls the different percentages a performance change without discussing their denominators.
return-denominator.principle: The numerator did not change in this example; the cash base did. Both percentages must carry their denominator definitions.
return-denominator.risk: A definition change can be mistaken for a change in operating outcome.
return-denominator.deliverable: the original numerator, both cash component schedules and a consistent label for each return measure

cash-flow-definition.subject: Operating bridge A
facts: The room-revenue illustration is $50,000 and operating costs are $25,000.
Annual debt payments are $24,000.
The headline calls the $25,000 operating surplus owner cash without subtracting the debt line.
cash-flow-definition.principle: Operating income and debt-adjusted cash flow are different measures. The stated figures leave $1,000 after the entered debt payments before other exclusions.
cash-flow-definition.risk: A useful operating metric can be overstated when described as all cash available to the owner.
cash-flow-definition.deliverable: a bridge from room revenue to operating income and then debt-adjusted cash, with additional exclusions stated

projected-versus-actual.subject: Mixed-status case A
facts: The example purchase price is a recorded transaction field in the scenario.
The room-revenue amount is a forward-looking assumption rather than an observed operating result.
The presentation combines the two without labeling their different evidence status.
projected-versus-actual.principle: An observed purchase input does not convert an assumed operating input into actual performance. The combined output remains a scenario.
projected-versus-actual.risk: Readers may infer that an entire result was observed when only one component was recorded.
projected-versus-actual.deliverable: a status label for every material field and separate treatment of recorded, quoted and assumed inputs

reporting-period.subject: Period alignment A
facts: The revenue report covers twelve months.
The expense export covers nine months and lacks a bridge for the remaining three.
The summary subtracts the nine-month expenses from the full-year revenue and labels the difference an annual result.
reporting-period.principle: The subtraction is possible mathematically but does not establish a like-for-like annual measure. The uncovered period must stay visible.
reporting-period.risk: An unaligned interval can overstate the apparent surplus without any arithmetic error.
reporting-period.deliverable: matching-period records or an explicit bridge labeling the unobserved interval and any estimate

client-stage-context.subject: Service-stage example A
facts: The retained account describes an introductory conversation and the questions discussed.
The later summary uses it as support for a completed acquisition and a year of operations.
No later-stage account or operating record is supplied in the example.
client-stage-context.principle: A source about one stage supports only the experience it actually addresses. Later results cannot be supplied by inference.
client-stage-context.risk: A narrow account can become an unsupported broad endorsement when its stage is omitted.
client-stage-context.deliverable: a stage-specific source reference and a summary limited to the observations actually provided

review-chronology.subject: Review timeline A
facts: The source metadata shows one original post and a later update by the same account.
The collection summary counts the update as a separate customer account.
The response sequence is omitted from the timeline.
review-chronology.principle: An update can change the context of one account without becoming another independent experience. Preserve the sequence and source identity.
review-chronology.risk: A timeline error can affect both the count and the interpretation of visible feedback.
review-chronology.deliverable: the original post, update history and response dates treated as one traceable source sequence

review-specificity.subject: Feedback scope A
facts: The source description concerns response speed during coordination.
The summary attributes a financial return claim that the source did not make.
No quoted or linked operating records support that added statement in the example.
review-specificity.principle: A summary must distinguish an explicit observation from the publisher's inference. Service communication and financial performance are different claim types.
review-specificity.risk: Added specificity can make feedback appear to establish an outcome it never discussed.
review-specificity.deliverable: a narrow paraphrase tied to the original source and separate evidence for any financial claim

review-incentives.subject: Solicitation record A
facts: The visible solicitation note asks for feedback but does not state an incentive in the supplied example.
A later summary asserts that a reward was provided without a supporting record.
The source register leaves the relationship field unresolved.
review-incentives.principle: The absence of a supplied relationship record does not establish either that an incentive existed or that it did not. Record what is disclosed and what remains unknown.
review-incentives.risk: An unresolved relationship can become an unsupported factual allegation if the summary fills the gap.
review-incentives.deliverable: the actual disclosure or solicitation terms and a conclusion limited to the available evidence

company-ownership.subject: Publisher disclosure A
facts: The hypothetical publication is owned by the company it discusses.
Its about page identifies that relationship.
A search-result description calls the publication independent without carrying the ownership context.
company-ownership.principle: Publisher identity is relevant to how a reader interprets evaluative material. A company perspective should not be presented as an independent assessment.
company-ownership.risk: A missing relationship label can change the apparent authority of an otherwise clearly attributed resource.
company-ownership.deliverable: a visible publisher statement and consistent ownership context in the page and its metadata

complaint-resolution.subject: Resolution timeline A
facts: The source sequence contains a concern and a response inviting further contact.
No documented completion step is supplied in the example.
The summary describes the concern as resolved based only on the invitation to contact support.
complaint-resolution.principle: A response, proposed action and documented completion are separate events. An invitation alone does not establish the final outcome.
complaint-resolution.risk: The summary can overstate resolution or imply fault if it treats an incomplete sequence as conclusive.
complaint-resolution.deliverable: the available follow-up sequence and a status that distinguishes proposed action from documented completion

scope-exclusion.subject: Service scope A
facts: The example proposal lists sourcing and transaction coordination.
A separate requested task is identified as outside that scope.
The service summary assumes that the excluded task was included without a documented change.
scope-exclusion.principle: Expectations and retained scope need to be compared directly. A general service label does not supply an omitted deliverable.
scope-exclusion.risk: An evidence review can misattribute an event when it ignores the actual scope boundary.
scope-exclusion.deliverable: the relevant scope, exclusions and any documented change, with professional review where interpretation is needed

responsibility-boundary.subject: Responsibility matrix A
facts: The acquisition scope ends at its stated handoff.
The ongoing operating task is assigned to a separate provider under another scope.
The summary treats both providers as one continuing obligation.
responsibility-boundary.principle: The specific event should be mapped to the actual role and relevant record. A shared project context does not merge separate scopes.
responsibility-boundary.risk: A broad brand-level conclusion can exceed what the source shows about the responsible task.
responsibility-boundary.deliverable: a task-to-provider map and the records governing the particular stage or event

marketing-timestamp.subject: Offer chronology A
facts: A dated proposal belongs to an earlier engagement period.
The current marketing page describes a later offer with different deliverables.
The comparison assumes the current page explains the earlier engagement without establishing that connection.
marketing-timestamp.principle: A current description and a past agreement can address different versions. The relevant period and scope must remain attached to each.
marketing-timestamp.risk: A timing mismatch can produce an unfair comparison even when both sources are accurately copied.
marketing-timestamp.deliverable: the dated source versions and a comparison limited to the actual period and engagement being discussed

source-traceability.subject: Source citation A
facts: The summary cites a company homepage rather than the document supporting its specific claim.
The source register has no document title, observation date or relevant section reference.
A copied figure is therefore not reproducible from the supplied citation alone.
source-traceability.principle: A link to a publisher is different from a link to the evidence for a particular statement. Traceability needs the actual record and context.
source-traceability.risk: Readers cannot repeat the comparison if the source reference stops at a broad landing page.
source-traceability.deliverable: a precise, authorized source reference with date, scope and the location of the relevant material
